Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, quick intro, im maya from Redwood, and with me is ethan, our solutions eng, could you do quick intros on your side Amir?
[00:06] Amir: yeah hi all this is Amir, im cto at CedralTide, we run the conversational assistant for field service, main question is throughput during morning spike, roughly 7am to 9am pst, and we saw big token bursts last month during a promo.
[00:14] Leah: and im Leah, we own model infra and quality, our SLO is p95 under 1.2s for full response for customer-facing chat. that includes stream so clinicians or agents get tokens as they arrive.
[00:22] Roberto: roberto here, infra, we have k8s clusters and a private subnet, not fully air-gapped but we need VPC/TLS and KMS integration for keys.
[00:28] Ethan: great, thanks. quick question to ground the convo, what models and token lengths are we seeing in production for your assistant?
[00:34] Leah: most sessions avg 120 tokens response, some up to 800 tokens for long instructions. models are 13B finetuned and also experimenting with 7B quantized for cost. concurrency during spikes around 140-170 concurrent streams.
[00:44] Maya: got it. so two important SLOs here: first-token latency and streaming p95 across the session. When you say p95 under 1.2s, is that time-to-first-token or time-to-complete?
[00:52] Leah: that 1.2s is to complete the visible response, but ideally first token <350ms so it feels snappy.
[00:57] [00:57] Amir: and cost matters, we cant triple our infra spend. so tradeoffs: accepting slightly higher p95 for smaller model or quantization is okay if quality holds.
[01:05] Ethan: good, that matches a lot we see. for our bench we measure both TTF (time to first) and stream tail p95, and also tokens-per-second sustained vs peak. can you characterize the burst pattern? is it a ramp or a sudden spike?
[01:15] Roberto: it's usually a sudden ingress when a scheduled job runs - within 30s we see a 3x increase and sustained for 10-20 minutes. additionally random smaller bursts throughout the hour.
[01:25] Maya: ok we generally recommend testing two scenarios: steady-state concurrency (e.g., 150) for 30-60m and a burst scenario that ramps from 20 to 180 in 30s to measure failovers, fallbacks, and queueing. we also track token/s because for streaming long responses token emission rate and tail p95 matter.
[01:37] Leah: what numbers should we expect for 13B fp16 vs 7B int8? ballpark token/sec and p95?
[01:44] Ethan: ballpark, on a single A100-class GPU with optimized kernels, for 13B fp16 you might see first-token p95 around 400-700ms depending on prompt and kv warmup; streaming token emission steady-state maybe 15-25 tokens/sec. 7B int8 can drop first token to 200-350ms and token/sec up to 30-45. those are rough of course and depend on sequence length, kv cache hit rate, and batching window.
[02:04] Amir: okay, our expected peak tokens/sec requirement if everyone asks for long responses could hit ~800 tokens/sec across the fleet during promo. how would Redwood handle that?
[02:12] Maya: two levers: dedicated pools and autoscale for steady growth, and burst capacity for transient spikes. we also have intelligent routing to cheaper model variants if capacity is constrained. for private deployments you can run the same runtime but in your VPC.
[02:23] Roberto: about network and KMS - do you support HSM-backed keys and CMEK?
[02:28] Ethan: yes we integrate with customer KMS and support CMEK for private. for hosted we offer managed KMS but can integrate with customer-managed where needed, we will send SOC2 plus network diagrams.
[02:36] Leah: in terms of measurement, we need both p95 for first token and p95 for token emission (like time between tokens? or last-token latency). how do you recommend we report streaming p95?
[02:46] Ethan: we capture both: first-token p95 and last-token p95 (response completion). for streaming we also measure inter-token jitter and tokens/sec over sliding windows to catch stalls. we include KV-cache warmup times separately in the report.
[02:59] Amir: what about cold starts when kv cache is empty? we occasionally see a degradation after a deploy.
[03:05] Maya: we have prefix caching and warm start strategies; for canary rollouts you can pin traffic so you don't flush caches across the board. we also can advise on pre-warming common prompts.
[03:13] Roberto: for the pilot we likely want Dedicated, is there a small reserved footprint we can use? e.g., 2 GPU nodes to test?
[03:18] Ethan: yes we can provision a small Dedicated pool for pilot — typically 2xA100 or equivalent — that should let you run a representative load. for large sustained production you can scale horizontally.
[03:26] Leah: in the pilot can you run our finetuned 13B? do you support loading customer checkpoints and quantizing them?
[03:31] Ethan: yes we support loading customer model artifacts and we have quantization paths in our runtime. we recommend testing both the original fp16 and a tuned int8 quantized variant in the pilot to see quality vs latency tradeoffs.
[03:40] [03:40] Amir: what telemetry will we get? we need per-request tracing, token-level cost, and per-model p95 dashboards.
[03:46] Maya: Redwood Console includes per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost breakdowns, latency histograms, and traces. we'll share a sample dashboard export and the retention policy options.
[03:54] Leah: great. one more question — regulatory: can we run the control plane in our VPC and data plane on-prem? some of our clients require that separation.
[04:01] Ethan: we do a private deployment option: control plane can be customer-managed with the runtime in your network. for air-gapped setups we have an on-prem package too; we'll include the architecture note.
[04:09] Maya: ok to move to what we'll do next — benchmark plan. our typical approach: 1) you give us 3 prompt sets (short, medium, long) and concurrency windows; 2) we run a baseline against hosted quick tests for initial estimates; 3) Dedicated pilot with your artifacts for 48-72h steady-state and burst windows; 4) deliver p95-first-token and p95-completion numbers, tokens/sec steady and peak, and recommendations (batching/windowing/quant).
[04:30] Amir: timeline? we want results before our board meeting mid-Oct.
[04:33] Maya: we can start pilot week of Oct 10 and aim to deliver an initial report within 7 business days after pilot completion.
[04:40] Roberto: regarding failure modes, we want to see graceful degradation — prefer fallback to smaller model instead of 503s. does Redwood support that?
[04:47] Ethan: yes — routing policies allow fallback to compatible model variants by policy, and we can simulate capacity restrictions in the pilot.
[04:53] [04:53] Leah: any known gotchas when measuring streaming p95 vs non-streaming generation?
[04:58] Ethan: yes, measurement semantics differ: streaming TTF is usually smaller because you get the first token sooner but the last-token p95 depends on throughput per token and network jitter. also batching windows that increase throughput can add small startup delay, so we report both.
[05:12] Maya: ok actions — we'll send the test harness repo link and a short spreadsheet where you fill expected concurrency and prompt distribution, and we'll schedule the pilot kickoff.
[05:20] Amir: perfect. also can you include rough cost estimation for two scenarios: sustained 150 concurrency 13B fp16 vs 7B int8 with burst 180?
[05:28] Maya: yes will include in the pricing sheet.
[05:31] Ethan: I'll prepare the sample bench config with headers: ramp profile, steady state, bursts, and what metrics we'll record.
[05:36] Leah: okay anything else?
[05:38] [05:38] Roberto: one small note, on our side we'll need an IP allowlist and a service account with scoped keys for the pilot.
[05:44] Maya: noted. we'll include network config steps in the doc.
[05:47] Amir: wrap up, thanks — excited to see the numbers.
[05:50] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with next steps and docs.
